# Introduction

This document includes the quality control of the different microarray pre-processing steps generated in the first R markdown script (*01_Preprocessing.Rmd*). We will use the different generated RData files of the first script as input for all the neccessary quality control and plot generation procedures. Following steps will be performed: 

1. Evaluate phenotype data
2. Quality control of raw data (chip scan date, boxplot, PCA plots, arrayQualityMetrics)
3. Quality control of calibrated data (boxplot, PCA plots, arrayQualityMetrics)
4. Quality control of calibrated and annotated data (boxplot, PCA plots, arrayQualityMetrics)
5. Quality control of batch corrected data (boxplot, PCA plots, arrayQualityMetrics)

We will also generate several RData files for the different quality control steps, as some of them include long processing times.  

# Packages 

Below you can find the list of packages that are required by the workflow. 

```{r}
# Quality control packages 
library(oligo) # for background correction, normalization and summarization
library(arrayQualityMetrics) # for quality control
library(psych)

# Plotting and colour option packages
library(ggplot2) # for (PCA) plots
library(ggrepel) # add nicer text to ggplots
library(GGally) # for mds plot
library(ggpubr) # multiple ggplots on one page
library(corrplot)
library(devtools)
library(cowplot)
library(viridis) # for colorblind color palette
```

# Load Raw and Phenotype Data

For the data evaluation and pre-processing, we first will load the raw data files.

```{r}
load("/storage/groups/ccm01/workspace/MPIP-Dean_postmortem_brain/RData_Files/1_affymetrix_exon_microarray_raw_data.RData")
```

# Evaluate Phenotype Data

## Check Variables

First, we will look more closely into our phenotype data. The five replicates and three missing pH values were already removed in the preprocessing step. Now, we have `r length(pData$IID)` samples, including `r length(pData[pData$Dx == "SCZ", "Dx"])` schizophrenia, `r length(pData[pData$Dx == "BPD", "Dx"])` bipolar disorder, `r length(pData[pData$Dx == "MDD", "Dx"])` major depression disorder patients and `r length(pData[pData$Dx == "CTL", "Dx"])` healthy controls. 

One of the most important covariates is the post mortem interval (PMI) giving the time in hours from the death of a person until the removal of the samples. Another important covariate is the RNA integrity number (RIN), which tells us the quality of the RNA samples and should always be higher than six. The phenotype data also includes the age at death (Age), Sex, Diagnosis (Dx), pH, suicide information, ... (DOI), batch information, ancestry and some file identifier. The ancestry information was not available for all samples, which is the reason, why we used the genotype data to calculate the ancestry information (mds). We also distributed the files into three different batches according to their filename. File batch "a" includes all samples measured in 2009. File batch "9" and "M" include all samples measured in 2014.

A short summary of the most important phenotype variables:

```{r, echo = F}
pData <- pData(rawData)
summary(pData[, c("Age", "Sex", "Dx", "pH", "PMI", "Suicide", "Type_of_Death", "DOI", "RIN", "Batch", "Ancestry", "File")])
# add disease column to Data, where SCZ, BPD and MDD are all grouped into DIS
pData$DIS <- "DIS"
pData[pData$Dx == "CTL", "DIS"] <- "CTL"
# get six colors (for plots)
col <- viridis(20)
```

Now, we will check the covariates visually.

### Age

We will first check, how the Age is distributed in the complete dataset (ALL) and then check die distribution in the controls (CTL) and the patients - once SCZ, BP and MDD together (DIS) and then SCZ, BP and MDD alone. 

```{r, echo = F}
par(mfrow = c(3, 2))
hist(pData$Age, col = col[1], main = "Age Frequency", xlab = "Age")
hist(pData[pData$Dx == "CTL", "Age"], col = col[4], main = "Age Frequency (CTL)", xlab = "Age")
hist(pData[pData$Dx %in% c("SCZ", "BPD", "MDD"), "Age"], col = col[7], main = "Age Frequency (DIS)", xlab = "Age")
hist(pData[pData$Dx == "SCZ", "Age"], col = col[10], main = "Age Frequency (SCZ)", xlab = "Age")
hist(pData[pData$Dx == "BPD", "Age"], col = col[15], main = "Age Frequency (BPD)", xlab = "Age")
hist(pData[pData$Dx == "MDD", "Age"], col = col[19], main = "Age Frequency (MDD)", xlab = "Age")
```

### Type of Death And Diagnosis Correlation

```{r, echo = F}
pData <- pData[!is.na(pData$C1), ]
head(pData)
dx.death <- pData[, c("Dx", "Type_of_Death")]
dx.death.t <- as.data.frame(table(dx.death))

# grouped barplot
ggplot(dx.death.t, aes(fill = Dx, y = Freq, x = Type_of_Death)) + 
  geom_bar(position = "dodge", stat = "identity")

# Stacked barplot
ggplot(dx.death.t, aes(fill = Type_of_Death, y = Freq, x = Dx)) + 
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") + 
  scale_fill_manual(values = viridis(4)) +
  theme(text = element_text(size = 18), axis.text.x = element_text(size = 16), axis.text.y = element_text(size = 16)) + 
  labs(x = "Diagnosis", y = "Frequency") + 
  labs(fill = "Type of Death")

# Stacked Percent barplot
ggplot(dx.death.t, aes(fill = Type_of_Death, y = Freq, x = Dx)) + 
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "fill") + 
  scale_fill_manual(values = viridis(4)) +
  theme(text = element_text(size = 18), axis.text.x = element_text(size = 16), axis.text.y = element_text(size = 16)) + 
  labs(x = "Diagnosis", y = "Frequency in Percent (%)") + 
  labs(fill = "Type of Death")

dx.suicide <- pData[, c("Dx", "Suicide")]
dx.suicide.t <- as.data.frame(table(dx.suicide))

# Stacked barplot
ggplot(dx.suicide.t, aes(fill = Suicide, y = Freq, x = Dx)) + 
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") + 
  scale_fill_manual(values = viridis(3)) +
  theme(text = element_text(size = 18), axis.text.x = element_text(size = 16), axis.text.y = element_text(size = 16)) + 
  labs(x = "Diagnosis", y = "Frequency") + 
  labs(fill = "Suicide")

# Stacked Percent barplot
ggplot(dx.suicide.t, aes(fill = Suicide, y = Freq, x = Dx)) + 
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "fill") + 
  scale_fill_manual(values = viridis(3)) +
  theme(text = element_text(size = 18), axis.text.x = element_text(size = 16), axis.text.y = element_text(size = 16)) + 
  labs(x = "Diagnosis", y = "Frequency in Percent (%)") + 
  labs(fill = "Suicide")


# combined barplots
nat <- data.frame(sort(pData[pData$Type_of_Death == "Natural", "Age"]))
vio <- data.frame(sort(pData[pData$Type_of_Death == "Violent", "Age"]))
nvio <- data.frame(sort(pData[pData$Type_of_Death == "Non-violent", "Age"]))
colnames(nat) <- "Age"
colnames(vio) <- "Age"
colnames(nvio) <- "Age"
nat$Type_of_Death <- "Natural"
vio$Type_of_Death <- "Violent"
nvio$Type_of_Death <- "Non-violent"
tod.combined <- rbind(nat, vio, nvio)
# Histogram density plot
ggplot(tod.combined, aes(x = Age, group = Type_of_Death, fill = Type_of_Death, colour = Type_of_Death)) + theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)) + labs(x = "Age", y = "Density") + stat_bin(colour = "gray", breaks = seq(10, 90, by = 10), alpha = 0.5, position = "identity", aes(y = ..density..)) + geom_density(fill = NA, size = 1.5) + theme_classic(base_size = 20) + scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0), limits = c(0, 100)) + scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) + scale_color_manual(values = viridis(4)) + scale_fill_manual(values = viridis(4)) 
```

### Age and Suicide Correlation

We found out, that especially young people are committing suicide. Here, we will show the suicide and no suicide correlation to the age of the patients. As none of the controls comitted suicide, we will not include them in the plot. (The plot looks strange including controls...)

```{r, echo = F}
# combined barplots
sui <- data.frame(sort(pData[pData$Suicide == "Y" & pData$Dx != "CTL", "Age"]))
nsui <- data.frame(sort(pData[pData$Suicide == "N" & pData$Dx != "CTL", "Age"]))
colnames(sui) <- "Age"
colnames(nsui) <- "Age"
sui$Suicide <- "Yes"
nsui$Suicide <- "No"
sui.combined <- rbind(sui, nsui)
# Histogram density plot
ggplot(sui.combined, aes(x = Age, group = Suicide, fill = Suicide, colour = Suicide)) + theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)) + labs(x = "Age", y = "Density") + stat_bin(colour = "gray", breaks = seq(10, 90, by = 10), alpha = 0.5, position = "identity", aes(y = ..density..)) + geom_density(fill = NA, size = 1.5) + theme_classic(base_size = 20) + scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0), limits = c(0, 100)) + scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) + scale_color_manual(values = viridis(4)) + scale_fill_manual(values = viridis(4))
```

Plot with control data as extra histogram:

```{r, echo = F}
sui <- data.frame(sort(pData[pData$Suicide == "Y" & pData$Dx != "CTL", "Age"]))
nsui <- data.frame(sort(pData[pData$Suicide == "N" & pData$Dx != "CTL", "Age"]))
ctl <- data.frame(sort(pData[pData$Suicide == "N" & pData$Dx == "CTL", "Age"]))
colnames(sui) <- "Age"
colnames(nsui) <- "Age"
colnames(ctl) <- "Age"
sui$Type <- "Suicide (DIS)"
nsui$Type <- "No Suicide (DIS)"
ctl$Type <- "No Suicide (CTL)"
sui.combined <- rbind(sui, nsui, ctl)
# Histogram density plot
ggplot(sui.combined, aes(x = Age, group = Type, fill = Type, colour = Type)) + labs(title = "Histogram: Suicide and Age Correlation") + theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)) + labs(x = "Age", y = "Density") + stat_bin(colour = "gray", breaks = seq(10, 90, by = 10), alpha = 0.5, position = "dodge", aes(y = ..density..)) + geom_density(fill = NA) + theme()
```

### Sex

Distribution in the Sex variable (ALL, CTL, DIS, SCZ).

```{r, echo = F}
#par(mfrow = c(2, 3))
#barplot(table(pData$Sex), col = "darkblue", main = "Sex Distribution")
#barplot(table(pData[pData$Dx == "CTL", "Sex"]), col = "darkgreen", main = "Sex Distribution (CTL)")
#barplot(table(pData[pData$Dx %in% c("SCZ", "BPD", "MDD"), "Sex"]), col = "darkred", main = "Sex Distribution (DIS)")
#barplot(table(pData[pData$Dx == "SCZ", "Sex"]), col = "red", main = "Sex Distribution (SCZ)")
#barplot(table(pData[pData$Dx == "BPD", "Sex"]), col = "red3", main = "Sex Distribution (BPD)")
#barplot(table(pData[pData$Dx == "MDD", "Sex"]), col = "red4", main = "Sex Distribution (MDD)")
plot.data <- rbind(as.data.frame(table(pData$Sex)), as.data.frame(table(pData[pData$Dx == "CTL", "Sex"])), as.data.frame(table(pData[pData$Dx %in% c("SCZ", "BPD", "MDD"), "Sex"])), as.data.frame(table(pData[pData$Dx == "SCZ", "Sex"])), as.data.frame(table(pData[pData$Dx == "BPD", "Sex"])), as.data.frame(table(pData[pData$Dx == "MDD", "Sex"])))
plot.data$Type <- c("ALL", "ALL", "CTL", "CTL", "DIS", "DIS", "SCZ", "SCZ", "BPD", "BPD", "MDD", "MDD")
plot.data$Gender <- "Male"
plot.data[plot.data$Var1 == "F", "Gender"] <- "Female"
plot.data$Type <- factor(plot.data$Type, levels = c("ALL", "CTL", "DIS", "SCZ", "BPD", "MDD"))
ggplot(plot.data) +
  # add bar for each discipline colored by gender
  geom_bar(aes(x = Type, y = Freq, fill = Gender),
           stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
  # name axes and remove gap between bars and y-axis
  scale_y_continuous("Counts", expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_x_discrete("") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(col[3], col[2])) +
  # remove grey theme
  theme_classic(base_size = 18) +
  # rotate x-axis and remove superfluous axis elements
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 0.5, vjust = 0.5),
        axis.ticks.x = element_blank()) 
```

We can see, that we have more than threefold of males in healthy controls and schizophrenia patients and slightly more females with bipolar disorder and major depression disorder. 

### Diagnosis (Dx)

```{r, echo = F}
par(mfrow = c(1,1))
barplot(table(pData$Dx), col = c(col[1], col[2], col[3], col[4]), main = "Barplot Diagnosis")
```

We have almost as many healthy controls as schizophrenia patients. The number of bipolar disorder and major despression disorder patients is relatively small compared to the amount of schizophrenia patients. 

### pH

```{r, echo = F}
par(mfrow = c(3, 2))
hist(pData$pH, col = col[1], main = "pH Frequency", xlab = "pH values")
hist(pData[pData$Dx == "CTL", "pH"], col = col[2], main = "pH Frequency (CTL)", xlab = "pH values")
hist(pData[pData$Dx %in% c("SCZ", "BPD", "MDD"), "pH"], col = col[3], main = "pH Frequency (DIS)", xlab = "pH values")
hist(pData[pData$Dx == "SCZ", "pH"], col = col[4], main = "pH Frequency (SCZ)", xlab = "pH values")
hist(pData[pData$Dx == "BPD", "pH"], col = col[5], main = "pH Frequency (BPD)", xlab = "pH values")
hist(pData[pData$Dx == "MDD", "pH"], col = col[6], main = "pH Frequency (MDD)", xlab = "pH values")
```

The pH has a peak around 6.4 to 6.6 in all different diagnosis types (including controls). 

### Postmortem Intervall (PMI)

```{r, echo = F}
par(mfrow = c(3, 2))
hist(pData$PMI, col = col[1], main = "PMI Frequency", xlab = "PMI values")
hist(pData[pData$Dx == "CTL", "PMI"], col = col[2], main = "PMI Frequency (CTL)", xlab = "PMI values")
hist(pData[pData$Dx %in% c("SCZ", "BPD", "MDD"), "PMI"], col = col[3], main = "PMI Frequency (DIS)", xlab = "PMI values")
hist(pData[pData$Dx == "SCZ", "PMI"], col = col[4], main = "PMI Frequency (SCZ)", xlab = "PMI values")
hist(pData[pData$Dx == "BPD", "PMI"], col = col[5], main = "PMI Frequency (BPD)", xlab = "PMI values")
hist(pData[pData$Dx == "MDD", "PMI"], col = col[6], main = "PMI Frequency (MDD)", xlab = "PMI values")
```

The highest peak of PMI in the samples lieas around 40 to 50 hours (~ 2 days) after death. In the controls and major depression disorder, we can see, that some of the samples were taken earlier (around 1 day after death). 

### Suicide

In the phenotype data we also have the information given, if the patients performed suicide (y) or not (n). None of the healthy controls committed suicide.  

```{r, echo = F}
#par(mfrow = c(2, 3))
#barplot(table(pData$Suicide), col = "darkblue", main = "Suicide Distribution")
#barplot(table(pData[pData$Dx == "CTL", "Suicide"]), col = "darkgreen", main = "Suicide Distribution (CTL)")
#barplot(table(pData[pData$Dx %in% c("SCZ", "BPD", "MDD"), "Suicide"]), col = "darkred", main = "Suicide Distribution (DIS)")
#barplot(table(pData[pData$Dx == "SCZ", "Suicide"]), col = "red", main = "Suicide Distribution (SCZ)")
#barplot(table(pData[pData$Dx == "BPD", "Suicide"]), col = "red3", main = "Suicide Distribution (BPD)")
#barplot(table(pData[pData$Dx == "MDD", "Suicide"]), col = "red4", main = "Suicide Distribution (MDD)")
plot.data <- rbind(as.data.frame(table(pData$Suicide)), as.data.frame(table(pData[pData$Dx == "CTL", "Suicide"])), as.data.frame(table(pData[pData$Dx %in% c("SCZ", "BPD", "MDD"), "Suicide"])), as.data.frame(table(pData[pData$Dx == "SCZ", "Suicide"])), as.data.frame(table(pData[pData$Dx == "BPD", "Suicide"])), as.data.frame(table(pData[pData$Dx == "MDD", "Suicide"])))
plot.data$Type <- c("ALL", "ALL", "CTL", "CTL", "DIS", "DIS", "SCZ", "SCZ", "BPD", "BPD", "MDD", "MDD")
plot.data$Suicide <- "Yes"
plot.data[plot.data$Var1 == "N", "Suicide"] <- "No"
plot.data$Type <- factor(plot.data$Type, levels = c("ALL", "CTL", "DIS", "SCZ", "BPD", "MDD"))
ggplot(plot.data) +
  # add bar for each discipline colored by gender
  geom_bar(aes(x = Type, y = Freq, fill = Suicide),
           stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
  # name axes and remove gap between bars and y-axis
  scale_y_continuous("Counts", expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_x_discrete("") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(col[3], col[2])) +
  # remove grey theme
  theme_classic(base_size = 18) +
  # rotate x-axis and remove superfluous axis elements
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 0.5, vjust = 0.5),
        axis.ticks.x = element_blank()) 
```

We can see, that most of the major depression disorder (MDD) patients were doing suicide, whereas only half of the schizophrenia and bipolar disorder patients were performing suicide. All healthy controls died on a natural cause.

### DOI

What does DOI stand for?!? For the complete disease samples the histogram looks exactly like the histogram for the complete dataset, as none of the controls has any DOI information given. 

```{r, echo = F}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
doi = pData[!is.na(pData$DOI), ] # get samples with DOI infos (without NA's included)
#hist(doi$DOI, col = "darkblue", main = "DOI Frequency", xlab = "DOI values")
#hist(doi[doi$Dx == "CTL", "DOI"], col = "darkgreen", main = "DOI Frequency (CTL)", xlab = "DOI values")
hist(doi[doi$Dx %in% c("SCZ", "BPD", "MDD"), "DOI"], col = col[1], main = "DOI Frequency (DIS)", xlab = "DOI values")
hist(doi[doi$Dx == "SCZ", "DOI"], col = col[2], main = "DOI Frequency (SCZ)", xlab = "DOI values")
hist(doi[doi$Dx == "BPD", "DOI"], col = col[3], main = "DOI Frequency (BPD)", xlab = "DOI values")
hist(doi[doi$Dx == "MDD", "DOI"], col = col[4], main = "DOI Frequency (MDD)", xlab = "DOI values")
```

### RNA Integrity Number (RIN)

```{r, echo = F}
par(mfrow = c(3, 2))
hist(pData$RIN, col = col[1], main = "RIN Frequency", xlab = "RIN values")
hist(pData[pData$Dx == "CTL", "RIN"], col = col[2], main = "RIN Frequency (CTL)", xlab = "RIN values")
hist(pData[pData$Dx %in% c("SCZ", "BPD", "MDD"), "RIN"], col = col[3], main = "RIN Frequency (DIS)", xlab = "RIN values")
hist(pData[pData$Dx == "SCZ", "RIN"], col = col[4], main = "RIN Frequency (SCZ)", xlab = "RIN values")
hist(pData[pData$Dx == "BPD", "RIN"], col = col[5], main = "RIN Frequency (BPD)", xlab = "RIN values")
hist(pData[pData$Dx == "MDD", "RIN"], col = col[6], main = "RIN Frequency (MDD)", xlab = "RIN values")
```

Most of the RNA integrity numbers lies between seven and eight. The data was already filtered for low RNA integrity numbers as we do not have any RIN below a value of six.

### Batch

```{r, echo = F}
#par(mfrow = c(2, 3))
#barplot(table(pData$Batch), col = "darkblue", main = "Batch Distribution")
#barplot(table(pData[pData$Dx == "CTL", "Batch"]), col = "darkgreen", main = "Batch Distribution (CTL)")
#barplot(table(pData[pData$Dx %in% c("SCZ", "BPD", "MDD"), "Batch"]), col = "darkred", main = "Batch Distribution (DIS)")
#barplot(table(pData[pData$Dx == "SCZ", "Batch"]), col = "red", main = "Batch Distribution (SCZ)")
#barplot(table(pData[pData$Dx == "BPD", "Batch"]), col = "red3", main = "Batch Distribution (BPD)")
#barplot(table(pData[pData$Dx == "MDD", "Batch"]), col = "red4", main = "Batch Distribution (MDD)")
plot.data <- rbind(as.data.frame(table(pData$Batch)), as.data.frame(table(pData[pData$Dx == "CTL", "Batch"])), as.data.frame(table(pData[pData$Dx %in% c("SCZ", "BPD", "MDD"), "Batch"])), as.data.frame(table(pData[pData$Dx == "SCZ", "Batch"])), as.data.frame(table(pData[pData$Dx == "BPD", "Batch"])), as.data.frame(table(pData[pData$Dx == "MDD", "Batch"])))
plot.data$Type <- c(rep("ALL", 5), rep("CTL", 5), rep("DIS", 5), rep("SCZ", 5), rep("BPD", 5), rep("MDD", 5))
plot.data$Type <- factor(plot.data$Type, levels = c("ALL", "CTL", "DIS", "SCZ", "BPD", "MDD"))
plot.data$Var1 <- factor(plot.data$Var1, levels = c("A", "1", "2", "3", "4"))
ggplot(plot.data) +
  # add bar for each discipline colored by gender
  geom_bar(aes(x = Type, y = Freq, fill = Var1),
           stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
  # name axes and remove gap between bars and y-axis
  scale_y_continuous("Counts", expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_x_discrete("") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = viridis(5)) +
  # remove grey theme
  theme_classic(base_size = 18) +
  # rotate x-axis and remove superfluous axis elements
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 0.5, vjust = 0.5),
        axis.ticks.x = element_blank()) 
```

Most of the samples were measured in batch 1 and 2. Some also in batch A and a really small number in the batches 3 and 4. We can see, that the samples in batch A only include schizophrenia patients and controls. The bipolar disorder patients are only included in batch 1 and 2.

We are still not sure, how the samples were distributed into the different batches, as the sample date generation does not match with the batch numbers (see section "Plot sample generation dates" below).

### Ancestry 

```{r, echo = F}
#par(mfrow = c(2, 3))
#barplot(table(pData$Ancestry), col = "darkblue", main = "Ancestry Distribution")

#barplot(table(pData[pData$Dx == "BPD", "Ancestry"]), col = "red3", main = "Ancestry Distribution (BPD)")
#barplot(table(pData[pData$Dx == "MDD", "Ancestry"]), col = "red4", main = "Ancestry Distribution (MDD)")
plot.data <- rbind(as.data.frame(table(pData$Ancestry)), as.data.frame(table(pData[pData$Dx == "CTL", "Ancestry"])), as.data.frame(table(pData[pData$Dx %in% c("SCZ", "BPD", "MDD"), "Ancestry"])), as.data.frame(table(pData[pData$Dx == "SCZ", "Ancestry"])), as.data.frame(table(pData[pData$Dx == "BPD", "Ancestry"])), as.data.frame(table(pData[pData$Dx == "MDD", "Ancestry"])))
plot.data$Type <- c(rep("ALL", 4), rep("CTL", 4), rep("DIS", 4), rep("SCZ", 4), rep("BPD", 4), rep("MDD", 4))
plot.data$Type <- factor(plot.data$Type, levels = c("ALL", "CTL", "DIS", "SCZ", "BPD", "MDD"))
ggplot(plot.data) +
  # add bar for each discipline colored by gender
  geom_bar(aes(x = Type, y = Freq, fill = Var1),
           stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
  # name axes and remove gap between bars and y-axis
  scale_y_continuous("Counts", expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_x_discrete("") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = viridis(4)) +
  # remove grey theme
  theme_classic(base_size = 18) +
  # rotate x-axis and remove superfluous axis elements
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 0.5, vjust = 0.5),
        axis.ticks.x = element_blank()) 
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

It is interesting, that all bipolar disorder and major depression disorder samples have an unknown ancestry. Most of the other samples are Ceucasian (CEU) and only a small amount is Chinese (CHB). Both types can be found in the control and schizophrenia samples. Only one schizophrenia samples has no ancestry information and the unique CEU/CHB sample is also a schizophrenia case.

### Correlation Plot

```{r, echo = F}
# remove identifier columns (MHRIID, Filenamne, File, Batch and ShortName)
pData.new <- pData[, -which(names(pData) %in% c("MHRIID", "Filename", "File", "ShortName", "Batch", "FID", "SOL", "IID", "pH_old", "Cause_of_Death", "Ancestry", "DOI", "Chip", "DIS", "Suicide"))]
# change BPD and MDD diagnosis (Dx) to AFF
pData.new$Dx <- as.character(pData.new$Dx) # change factor column to character
pData.new[pData.new$Dx == "BPD" | pData.new$Dx == "MDD", "Dx"] <- "SCZ" # change BPD and MDD to SCZ
pData.new[, c("Sex", "Dx", "Suicide")] <- lapply(pData.new[, c("Sex", "Dx", "Suicide")], factor)
#sapply(pData.new, class) # check type of columns
# relevel disease (Dx) to control (CTL)
pData.new$Dx <- factor(pData.new$Dx, levels = c("CTL", "SCZ"))
# save categorical and continuous variable names
classes <- sapply(pData.new, class) # get type of columns
categorical.cov = names(classes[classes == "factor"])
continuous.cov = names(classes[classes == "numeric"])
# generate contrast for design matrix
contrast <- lapply(categorical.cov, function(x) {fac = pData.new[, x]; return(contrasts(fac))})
names(contrast) <- categorical.cov
# generate design matrix
design <- model.matrix(~ . + Age + Sex + Dx + pH + PMI + RIN + Type_of_Death + C1 + C2 + C3 + C4, pData.new, contrasts.arg = contrast)
design.cor <- corr.test(design[, -1], use='pairwise.complete.obs', method = "pearson", adjust = "none")
corrplot(design.cor$r, method = "circle", col = viridis(200, direction = -1))
```

## Check MDS (C1-C10)

First, we will check the mds values (C1-C10) of the genotypes given in the phenotype data. For some samples (`r length(is.na(pData$C1))`), we do not have any mds values given. 

```{r, echo = F}
# check mds
pData.new <- pData[, c(13, 20:29)]
pData.new[, c(2:11)] <- apply(pData.new[, c(2:11)], 2, function(x) as.numeric(as.character(x)))
pData.new <- pData.new[-c(which(is.na(pData.new$C1))), ] # remove rows with NA in C1
pData.new[pData.new$Ancestry == "", "Ancestry"] <- "NA" # set all empty ancestry values to NA
pData.new <- pData.new[order(pData.new$Ancestry),] # sort for ancestry type
ggpairs(pData.new, mapping = aes(colour = Ancestry), cardinality_threshold = 178)
```

We can not find any outliers in the figure above, so we will not remove any further samples from the dataset.

## Check MDS Eigenvalues

To find out, which of the 10 mds C-values have an impact on the samples and should be included as covariates in our model, we first need to plot (scree plot) their eigenvalues.   

```{r, echo = F}
mds.eigenval <- read.csv2("/storage/groups/ccm01/datasets/2018_MPIP-Dean_postmortem_brain/dean.eigenval", stringsAsFactors = F)
mds.eigenval <- apply(mds.eigenval, 1, function(x) as.numeric(x))
plot(mds.eigenval, type = "b", xlab = "MDS component", ylab = "Eigenvalue", col = col[1])
```

In the plot, we can see, that the biggest differences are between C1, C2, C3 and C4. After C4 the eigenvalues differ hardly, so we decided to only take C1 to C4 as covariates into account.

```{r, echo = F}
# get dates of newer files (2014)
dates <- rawData@protocolData@data$dates[grep("-", rawData@protocolData@data$dates)]
dates <- unlist(lapply(dates, function(x) strsplit(as.character(x), "T")[[1]][1]))
# get dates of older files (2009) and change to new format

# add all dates together
datesNew <- c(dates[0:90], as.character(betterDates), dates[91:length(dates)])
# sort dates
datesSorted <- datesNew[order(datesNew)]
datefreq <- table(as.Date(datesSorted, format='%Y-%m-%d'))
datefreq
plot(levels(factor(as.Date(datesSorted, format='%Y-%m-%d') - as.Date('2009-07-16'))), as.vector(datefreq), ylim = c(0, max(datefreq)), type='h', xlab='Days since start', ylab='No of arrays per day', main = "Dates - All Files", col = col[1])
# without 2009 samples
datesSorted <- datesSorted[41:length(datesSorted)] # remove 2009 samples
datefreq <- table(as.Date(datesSorted, format = '%Y-%m-%d'))
plot(levels(factor(as.Date(datesSorted, format='%Y-%m-%d') - as.Date('2014-06-06'))), as.vector(datefreq), ylim = c(0, max(datefreq)), type='h', xlab='Days since start', ylab='No of arrays per day', main = "Dates - 2014 Files", col = col[1])
rm(dates, dates2, betterDates, datesNew, datesSorted, datefreq)
```

## Boxplots

Now, we will represent the probe intensities in a boxplot graph, where each box corresponds to exactly one microarray sample. The boxplot function from the oligo package performs a log2-transformation by default, so we can use the boxplot function without any previous raw data transformation. The logarithmic scale simplifies the visualization of the data.

```{r, echo = F}
colors <- c(replicate(length(pData[pData$File == "9", "File"]), col[2]), replicate(length(pData[pData$File == "a", "File"]), col[5]), replicate(length(pData[pData$File == "M", "File"]), col[3]))
boxplot(rawData, target = "probeset", ylab = "log2 intensity", xlab = "Samples", las = 2, col = colors, main = "Boxplot of log2-intensities for the raw data")
```

Here, we can see that the density distributions of the individual samples are quite different, especially between the samples coming from the first cohort measured in 2009 (orange) compared to the second cohort measured in 2014 (cyan and pink). That is the reason, why we performed the RMA background correction, normalization and summarization step in the preprocessing pipeline. The boxplot for the normalized data will be shown in the next section. 

To also check the data on original intensity scale, we just need to set the transfo parameter to identity instead of the default log2. 

```{r, echo = F}
# with original intensities
boxplot(rawData, target = "probeset", transfo = identity, ylab = "Intensity", xlab = "Samples", las = 2, col = colors, main = "Boxplot of original intensities for the raw data")
```

You can see, that the plot using original intensities shows bigger differences than the plot using log2 transformed intensities and is making it more difficult to interpret the plot.

## PCA Plots

Before we can generate the different PCA plots, we need to calculate the log2 intensities of the raw data expression set as well as the first two principal components. 

```{r, echo = F, eval = F}
expRaw <- log2(exprs(rawData))	
PCAraw <- prcomp(t(expRaw), scale = FALSE)
percentVar <- round(100*PCAraw$sdev^2 / sum(PCAraw$sdev^2), 1)
sdRatio <- sqrt(percentVar[2] / percentVar[1])
dataRAW <- data.frame(PC1 = PCAraw$x[,1], PC2 = PCAraw$x[,2], Diagnosis = pData$Dx, Age = pData$Age, pH = pData$pH , 
                     File = pData$File, Sex = pData$Sex, Batch = pData$Batch, MHRI = pData$MHRIID, PMI = pData$PMI, 
                     Suicide = pData$Suicide, RIN = pData$RIN, ShortName = pData$ShortName, Ancestry = pData$Ancestry)
save(percentVar, sdRatio, dataRAW, file ="/storage/groups/ccm01/workspace/MPIP-Dean_postmortem_brain/RData_Files/5_affymetrix_exon_microarray_raw_data_for_PCA_plots.RData")
```

## arrayQualityMetrics

One easy way to do quality control of Microarray data is the use of the package arrayQualityMetrics. This package performs different quality control metrics and produces a html file including all generated plots and suggested samples to remove from the dataset. We will store the html file and check its output separately. 

```{r, eval = F}
rownames(pData) <- pData$ShortName
phenoData <- new("AnnotatedDataFrame", data = pData)
exprs <- exprs(rawData)
exampleSet <- ExpressionSet(assayData = exprs, phenoData = phenoData)
arrayQualityMetrics(expressionset = exampleSet, outdir = "/storage/groups/ccm01/workspace/MPIP-Dean_postmortem_brain/Figures/rawData/Report_before_rma", force = TRUE, do.logtransform = TRUE, intgroup = c("Dx"))
```

```{r, echo = F, fig.height = 10, fig.width = 10}
  scale_color_manual(values = c("brown", "red", "green", "darkorange2", "dodgerblue4"))
ggarrange(g1, g2, g3, g4, g5, g6, g7, g8, g9, g10, ncol = 2, nrow = 5)
```

## PC1-10 for the different covariates

```{r, echo = F}
pcr_rma <- prcomp(exprs_rma)
pcr_rma_rot <- pcr_rma$rotation
varnames =c("Age", "Sex", "PMI", "pH", "RIN", "Suicide", "Ancestry", "Dx", "Batch", "File")
vartype = c("continuous", "categorical", "continuous", "continuous", "continuous", "categorical", "categorical","categorical","categorical","categorical")
numPCs = 10  # Number of the top PCs to be used in subsequent association tests
results.assoc = results.pval = matrix(NA, nrow = length(varnames), ncol = numPCs)
colnames(results.assoc) = colnames(results.pval) = paste("PC", 1:numPCs, sep = "")
rownames(results.assoc) = rownames(results.pval) = varnames
for(i in 1:length(varnames)) {
  for(j in 1:numPCs) {
    if(vartype[i]  == "continuous") {
      fit = lm(pcr_rma_rot[,j]~pData[,varnames[i]])
      results.pval[i,j] = summary(fit)[[4]][[8]]
    }
    else if(vartype[i] == "categorical") {
      fit = aov(pcr_rma_rot[,j] ~ factor(pData[,varnames[i]]))
      results.pval[i,j] = summary(fit)[[1]][[5]][[1]]
    }
    results.assoc[i,] = results.pval[i,]
  }
}
results.assoc
rm(pcr_rma, pcr_rma_rot, varnames, vartype, numPCs, results.pval, results.assoc)
```

## PCA Plots

Exactly as for the PCA plots of the normalized data, we need to get the expression of the batch corrected data and calculate the first two principal components.

```{r, echo = F}
exprs_bc <- exprs(geneSummaries)
PCA_BC <- prcomp(t(exprs_bc), scale = FALSE)
percentVar <- round(100 * PCA_BC$sdev^2 / sum(PCA_BC$sdev^2), 1)
sd_ratio <- sqrt(percentVar[2] / percentVar[1])
dataB <- data.frame(PC1 = PCA_BC$x[,1], PC2 = PCA_BC$x[,2], Ancestry = pData$Ancestry, Diagnosis = pData$Dx, Age = pData$Age, 
                     pH = pData$pH , File = pData$File, Sex = pData$Sex, PMI = pData$PMI, Suicide = pData$Suicide, RIN = pData$RIN)
save(percentVar, sd_ratio, dataB, file ="/storage/groups/ccm01/workspace/MPIP-Dean_postmortem_brain/RData_Files/7_affymetrix_exon_microarray_data_after_rma_gene_summaries_annotated_combat_batch_corrected_for_PCA_plots.RData")
```
